title: 2,200-Year-Old Shipwreck Reveals Ancient Waterproofing Secrets
summary:
For thousands of years, sailors have needed to protect their wooden ships from water, salt, and hungry sea creatures. While we often focus on the wood itself, the non-wood materials used in ancient shipbuilding have been largely overlooked. A new study published in Frontiers in Materials is changing that.

Researchers in France and Croatia analyzed the protective coating on the Roman Republic shipwreck Ilovik-Paržine 1, which sank about 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern-day Croatia. They discovered two different waterproofing formulations: one made of pine tar (also called pitch) and another of pine tar mixed with beeswax.

"In archaeology, little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said lead author Dr. Armelle Charrié.

The mixture of beeswax and tar was known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa. It improves the adhesive's flexibility and is easier to apply when hot.

But the most fascinating part? Because pitch is naturally sticky, it captured pollen from the surrounding vegetation and preserved it for centuries. By analyzing the types of pollen, researchers could reconstruct the environment where the ship was built and repaired.

The pollen evidence pointed to a wide range of environments: Mediterranean coastal forests with holly oak and pine, shrublands with olive and hazel, riverbanks with alder and ash, and even mountainous areas with fir and beech. This suggests the ship was repaired in multiple locations across the Adriatic.

The vessel appears to have received four to five separate batches of coating over time. The stern and central section had the same material, while the bow had three distinct layers. This pattern indicates repeated repairs, with materials sourced from different regions.

Earlier research suggested the ship was built in Brundisium (modern Brindisi, Italy). The new pollen evidence supports that some coatings were applied there, while others were added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near where the wreck was found.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical."

This study not only reveals ancient waterproofing techniques but also shows how clever ancient shipbuilders were in adapting to their environment.
why_it_matters: This research shows that ancient technology was more adaptive and regionally connected than often assumed; studying overlooked materials can reveal where people traveled and how they maintained complex vehicles.

background_read: The Roman Republic was the period of ancient Rome before emperors, when Rome was already a busy Mediterranean power.
The Adriatic Sea is a long arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkan Peninsula; it holds many ancient shipwrecks, including Ilovik-Paržine 1, the wreck in this study.
Frontiers in Materials, the journal that published the research, is a peer-reviewed scientific journal focused on materials science and engineering.
Archaeologists have often paid less attention to organic coatings than to wooden hulls, even though waterproofing was essential for ancient navigation.

The sticky pitch on this ship trapped pollen, microscopic grains produced by plants, allowing scientists to reconstruct the coastal forests, shrublands, riverbanks, and mountain areas where repairs took place.
Brundisium, modern Brindisi in southeastern Italy, is the port where earlier research suggested the ship was built.
Pollen is useful because it survives in sticky materials and can be identified by plant type.

perspectives.description: Maritime archaeologists gain a new tool for tracing ancient repair routes and construction practices. The study demonstrates that materials once considered unimportant can hold detailed evidence about past technology.

The study points out that organic waterproofing materials have been largely overlooked. Ignoring these materials may have left gaps in our understanding of ancient shipbuilding and long-distance travel.

Pollen acts as an environmental proxy, turning trapped plant grains into a record of different landscapes. This shows how chemical and biological evidence can answer questions about movement and maintenance that wood alone cannot.
Similar analyses could be applied to other shipwrecks to map ancient trade and repair networks. Researchers may now pay closer attention to sticky coatings as archives of environmental history.
